strengths: Principled integration of domain-specific inductive bias: The use of aligned diffusion-map functional gradients as geometric node coordinates effectively addresses the challenge of representation collapse in dense, unthresholded functional connectivity graphs.

Well-designed architecture: The edge-conditioned graph transformer encoder combined with a memory-based cross-attention decoder enables compact graph-level bottleneck representations while successfully reconstructing full, dense, continuous-weighted matrices.

Comprehensive empirical validation: Evaluated across multiple dimensions, including edge reconstruction MSE, downstream cognitive state and stimulus decoding, clinical classification (BSNIP), and generative quality (MMD, 1-NN, edge KS, spectral KS, and topological statistics).

Thorough ablations and leakage-free setup: The paper systematically validates design choices (alignment, edge-conditioning, memory mechanism) across three parcellation granularities (64, 100, 150 nodes), and carefully ensures that the gradient template and normalization parameters are derived solely from training-set resting data.

Valuable neuroscientific interpretations: The analysis connecting latent geometric dispersion and directional variance (along the association-sensory axis) to cognitive performance aligns well with neuroscientific literature on neural efficiency and reconfiguration.
weaknesses: Scalability limitations: Because of the dense attention mechanism and $N \times N$ edge modulation, the approach is tested only on relatively low-resolution parcellations (up to 150 nodes), restricting direct applicability to fine-grained voxel/vertex-level connectomics.

Simplicity of the generative setup: Fitting a diffusion model over a low-dimensional vector space ($d_g = 16$ or $32$) is fairly standard; the generative quality largely hinges on the fidelity of the frozen deterministic decoder rather than graph diffusion dynamics.

Scope of clinical evaluation: Downstream diagnostic evaluation is limited to a single binary comparison (healthy control vs. schizophrenia on BSNIP); evaluating additional clinical cohorts or phenotypes would strengthen claims of general clinical utility.

strengths: Principled problem formulation: Directly learns from dense, signed, and weighted functional connectomes without arbitrary sparsification or thresholding, addressing key failure modes of traditional MPNNs (over-smoothing and representational collapse).

Sound methodological design: The integration of Procrustes-aligned diffusion-map functional gradients as low-frequency positional inductive biases into an edge-conditioned transformer encoder and memory-based cross-attention decoder is well-motivated and structurally sound.

Rigorous data leakage prevention: Strict experimental hygiene is maintained by computing both the parcellation clustering and the orthogonal Procrustes reference template exclusively from the resting-state training split.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: Tested across HCP (resting-state and 7 cognitive tasks) and BSNIP (clinical schizophrenia classification), benchmarking against relevant baselines (GAE, Graphite, GRALE, GATE, GraphMAE) across multiple parcellation scales (64, 100, 150 nodes).

Compelling multi-faceted extensions: Demonstrates clear utility beyond static reconstruction, including spatio-temporal fusion with GRUs for dynamic decoding, latent diffusion for synthetic connectome generation, and meaningful neuroscientific findings linking latent dispersion to cognitive performance.
weaknesses: Assumption of fixed node correspondence: The memory-based cross-attention decoding mechanism and node alignment rely strictly on a fixed atlas parcellation across subjects, precluding direct deployment to graphs with varying node sets or mismatched parcellations.

Scalability constraints: While efficient for standard coarse parcellations (64–150 nodes), maintaining dense edge tensors of size $N \times N \times d_e$ alongside full self-attention scales quadratically, making scaling to high-resolution atlases (e.g., Schaefer 400–1000) or voxel-level connectomes computationally intensive.

Scope of temporal extension: The neural dynamics extension is primarily validated on blocked working-memory fMRI segments; further validation across continuous resting-state dynamics and irregular task regimes would strengthen the dynamic modeling claims.

strengths: The paper addresses a significant and challenging problem in functional neuroimaging: learning compact, unsupervised graph-level representations directly from dense, weighted functional connectivity (FC) networks without arbitrary thresholding or sparsification.

The framework is conceptually coherent and tailored to neuroimaging properties: leveraging aligned diffusion-map functional gradients provides an effective inductive bias, while the edge-conditioned attention encoder and memory-based cross-attention decoder prevent representational collapse and enable accurate dense reconstruction.

The empirical evaluation is comprehensive and multi-faceted, spanning FC reconstruction, downstream cognitive/stimulus decoding, spatial-temporal modeling of neural dynamics, clinical phenotype classification (BSNIP), and generative quality assessment (latent diffusion evaluated via MMD, 1-NN two-sample tests, and spectral/topological KS tests).

Experimental protocols are methodologically rigorous with respect to data leakage: functional gradient templates and data-driven parcellations are strictly derived from the resting-state training split before being propagated to task states and validation/test folds.
weaknesses: From a core machine learning perspective, algorithmic originality is somewhat incremental. The individual technical components (edge-conditioned transformer layers following Ma et al., memory-augmented cross-attention, latent diffusion, and GRU dynamics fusion) represent integrations and adaptations of established architectures rather than fundamentally new learning paradigms.

The approach strictly relies on fixed node correspondence and shared parcellation across subjects. While standard in regional functional connectomics, this prevents transfer across different brain atlases, varying node sets, or unaligned graphs.

Scalability is bounded by dense full-attention: experiments are limited to relatively coarse parcellations (64 to 150 regions), which restricts applicability to high-resolution, dense vertex- or voxel-level functional networks.

While downstream task decoding is strong, clinical classification performance on BSNIP (AUC 0.737) remains modest, and evaluation lacks validation across independent acquisition sites and scanner cohorts to test out-of-distribution robustness.
The code availability link in the manuscript text contains an empty placeholder, which currently limits immediate reproducibility verification.
